project-oneliner: Runs a small farm's whole week — orders, delivery, collections — and tells it when to buy its next flock of hens
project-description:
A real farm outside Bogotá sells eggs, blackberries and honey to about 150 customers every week. It runs on a 59-sheet spreadsheet: someone clones a tab, reads WhatsApp to find out who is in or out this week, edits purchase orders by hand in Word, and once a month runs a macro to work out who owes money. Roughly $580.000 a month goes uncollected, and customers quietly fall off the delivery list.

Toromana replaces that. The weekly order builds itself from the standing customers and the three sellers edit it live; paused customers stay visible in grey with the reason instead of disappearing. The delivery list and the signed receipts print exactly as the paper they replace. Payments apply oldest-first, so the collections panel sorts itself by how long the money has been owed, with a pre-written WhatsApp message one tap away.

The part that is not a CRUD is the production planner. A flock does not lay evenly: it climbs to a peak, drops by half through a molt, returns to a second peak, then fades and is sold. Buying at the wrong moment stacks a new flock's trough on top of an old one's and leaves a worse hole than before. The planner fits that curve to the farm's own records — stating on screen how much of it comes from their data and how much from a species prior — and then searches purchase weeks and sizes to stagger flocks so one's peak covers another's trough. On the seeded barn it cuts weekly deviation from 568 to 119 eggs and finds a replacement cadence nobody encoded.

Built in nine hours on Next.js, Supabase and Vercel. Runs at $0 a month.
